subject: Business Models
title: Subscription Regulation
description: A short lesson to help you apply Subscription Regulation.

hook.text: The FTC's 'click to cancel' rule: canceling must be as easy as signing up. No more phone-call traps.

buildup.text: Governments worldwide are cracking down on dark patterns, auto-renewals, and hidden subscription terms.

discovery.text: California requires companies to show total cost before checkout—including all fees and recurring charges.

twist.text: Regulation might actually help good subscription companies. Transparent pricing rewards products people truly want.

climax.text: The era of 'trick them into staying' is ending. The future rewards genuine subscriber value.

punchline.text: Easy in, easy out. Regulation forces honesty into subscriptions.

quiz.question: What does the FTC's 'click to cancel' rule require?
options: Cancellation must be as easy as signup

details.summary: Subscription regulation encompasses laws governing automatic renewal disclosures, cancellation rights, and billing transparency. The FTC's click-to-cancel rule, California's automatic renewal law.
details.whyItMatters: Regulatory pressure is fundamentally changing subscription business practices. Companies that rely on sneaky retention tactics face enforcement actions and fines..
takeaways: Regulations require clear disclosure of automatic renewal terms and pricing
Click-to-cancel rules mandate cancellation be as easy as sign-up
Non-compliance risks significant fines and enforcement actions

faq.question: What are the key subscription regulations companies must comply with?
faq.answer: The FTC requires clear disclosure of material terms before purchase, affirmative consent to recurring charges, and simple cancellation procedures. California mandates online cancellation for online subscriptions. The EU requires pre-renewal reminders and easy withdrawal mechanisms.

faq.question: What penalties do companies face for subscription regulation violations?
faq.answer: The FTC can impose fines of thousands per violation, with each subscriber potentially representing a separate violation. ABCmouse paid $10 million for dark pattern cancellation practices. States can pursue additional penalties. Class action lawsuits add further financial risk.
